knowns.fact: Requirements and options as Zac framed them

Gitignored *.local.* files (pilot.local.md, local styles) sit physically under src/.claude/ in this repo through the symlinks. Git never ships them, but any install route that copies src/ from disk would. Keeping them out of a release is this epic's job (giget fetches from GitHub, so it holds as long as releases are cut from git)

Copy-in fits, plugin doesn't: plugins can't ship rules or permissions, wipe user edits on update and namespace skills; candidates are plain degit/giget copy-in, copy-in plus a hash-manifest update, or copier
knowns.answers: Install route: plugin marketplace, copy script or degit-style clone, given users must own and edit their copy?

knowns.fact: Copying src/ brings project-context/README.md along with .claude/, so an install gets the conventions doc without library init copying it
knowns.answers: How does project-context/README.md reach a user's install, and should library init copy it?

knowns.fact: Zac's upgrade ambition: a recorded installed version, an upgrade skill that merges upstream around local improvements, an escape hatch that warns before oversized upgrades, and a fast path for simple merges (the local changelog is parked, d10; pick-the-parts options are parked, d26)

install.sh lives at the repo root, outside src/, so the copy-in never ships it (spiked: install.sh never appears in an installed tree). A piped script can't see its own URL, so the version it installs has to be stamped in; that stamping now happens on the release asset (see the release-asset decision)
knowns.answers: Where does install.sh live and how is it fetched (repo root rather than src/, URL pinned to a release tag) so it never ships into installs itself?

knowns.fact: install.sh installs a full SHA and writes .claude/ang/version.json { ref, sha, installedAt }. Spiked: resolving the ref through GitHub's API and installing that SHA kept the record matching git rev-parse on every run. Under d28 the default install takes the SHA from its stamp instead of the API
knowns.answers: Where and in what form does an install record its Ang version (tag, commit SHA), and how does an upgrade baseline an instance with no record, such as ohnvm?

knowns.fact: A file-by-file three-way merge (base: the version.json SHA; git merge-file where both changed) sorts every file into one category. Across 28 upstream-changed files and 6 local improvements, only 4 files needed judgement. Conflicted files are the cost signal; fast-path and new-file counts are nearly free. Clean merges can still be semantically stale, and upstream moves look like deletions
knowns.answers: How would an upgrade skill merge upstream changes around local improvements: what makes a merge simple versus too much (the escape hatch), and what does taking only chosen parts look like?

knowns.fact: Minimum supported Node is the current LTS (long-term support release), Node 26 today, bumped each October with engines, .node-version and CI (open-source-hygiene d11). install.sh and the documented prerequisite check for >=26, not just that node exists
knowns.answers: What minimum Node version do the documented install prerequisite and install.sh's node check state? It waits on open-source-hygiene's u7: docs say 21+, but the code's import.meta.dirname needs 22.16+. install.sh itself needs only 18+ (fetch). Once it's settled, install.sh should check the version, not just that node exists

knowns.fact: Releases are git tags with generated GitHub Releases and no hand-kept changelog (open-source-hygiene d13). Generated notes can't declare moves or migrations, so u1's answer must come from something other than a changelog

Researched: semver at 0.x (minor bump for breaking changes pre-1.0). Copy-in tools (copier _migrations, Angular ng update) keep cumulative, version-keyed migration data in the versioned tree and run every step between installed and target, and none studied reads Release bodies at upgrade time. Every mainstream release tool needs Conventional Commits, changeset files or labelled PRs, so an LLM draft fits Ang. LLM-drafted notes exist (copilot-release-notes, communique) and always need human review. No install script studied checks that a ref is a release, so Ang's tags-only check is its own. Cheap to adopt: immutable releases, a release-body skeleton with Breaking changes first, per-version guidance, draft-then-publish. Not yet worth it: CHANGELOG.md, checksums, signing
knowns.answers: How do widely used open-source projects manage releases (versioning, changelog vs release notes, upgrade and migration guides, release assets, release tooling, install scripts pinned to tags), and where would Ang's release skill depart from that convention?

knowns.fact: Two separate per-version files at the repo root, outside src/: human release notes in releases/notes/vX.Y.Z.md (the GitHub Release body) and a formulaic agent-facing upgrade guide in releases/upgrades/vX.Y.Z.md, which the upgrade skill fetches on its own for every version in (installed, target]. Zac's call: the two have different readers, and mixing agent instructions into release notes reads as hacky
knowns.answers: Where the per-release upgrade guidance lives and what it contains: a GitHub Release asset, or a root-level release/ folder (outside src/) that holds each release's notes and upgrade guidance and feeds the Release body. Never inside src/. The upgrade skill already calls the releases API for its already-on-latest check. Depends on the release-practice research

knowns.fact: The fixture is a separate repo (e.g. zacbraddy/ang-upgrade-fixture), created by Zac during execution, guided by a story written for it (Zac's call)
knowns.answers: Where does the fixture repo live? Recommended: a separate repo (e.g. zacbraddy/ang-upgrade-fixture) that Zac creates, since its own git history is the point

knowns.fact: /cut-release runs: preflight warnings, then release-manifest and release-scout gather, then a version proposal Zac accepts or revises, then the notes and upgrade guide drafted and approved with Zac, then the fixture rehearsal, then commit, tag and push on an explicit go. A v* tag triggers the GitHub Actions job (tests, smoke install, stamp the install.sh asset, draft release). The skill opens the draft in the browser, Zac presses Publish, and post-publish checks follow (live one-liner install, fixture upgrade committed)
knowns.answers: What the release skill does, step by step: version scheme and bump, the log summary, the shape of the notes draft, the upgrade guidance spec, the install.sh stamp, tag and gh publish. Depends on the release-practice research and u1

knowns.fact: Spiked: a three-way JSON merge of settings.json (base: Ang's settings at the version.json SHA, fetched with the file-merge base) replaces changed Ang hooks and permissions with no duplicates or stale entries, keeps every user value and re-runs as a no-op. Arrays are sets of whole entries; a base entry missing from both sides is a conflict for the guided merge. With an empty base it reproduces the install merge (d7) exactly, so install and upgrade can share one implementation in the library script. No record degrades to the install merge (stale entries stay), which fits the escape hatch. outputStyle conflicts are noise to skip (tailor-ang owns it); key order may need normalising
knowns.answers: How does an upgrade update Ang's own settings entries without duplicating them? The user-favouring install merge would append a changed Ang hook beside the old one (candidate: diff against the previous release's settings.json found by the recorded SHA)

knowns.fact: A repo-only link script in a root scripts/ folder globs src/.claude/skills and src/.claude/agents, creates missing relative per-entry links and removes dangling ones, and re-runs as a no-op. A repo-only node --test fails on drift; it runs in the v* release CI job and /cut-release preflight lists drift as a warning. Not library validate: it ships, and this check is about the Ang repo's own layout (Zac's call)
knowns.answers: How are the per-entry symlinks for src/ skills and agents kept in step: a script that creates them by glob, and does library validate or a test flag a src/ entry with no link at the root?

knowns.fact: The fixture is seeded once, by hand, in the story that creates it, then rolled forward by real upgrades, so there is no maintained or deterministic seed generator (Zac's call: a reseeding setup would need no hosted repo). Any one-off script and its faker dependency stay in the fixture repo, never in Ang. Prose comes from faker, never an LLM. The seed is an rc.1 install plus: one local edit in every shipped area (skills, agents, rules, output-styles, scripts, ang/features, docs, project-context/README.md) so that upstream moves hit an edited file; the upgrade merge spike's five cases (a new local rule, an edit away from upstream's changes, an edit on a high-churn line, a new function in a shipped script, a custom setting plus a hook); a local-only skill and agent; a library built through ang-context-manager.mjs with an item at each stage, a 10k doc, a trigger and state entries, which is what tests library-convention migrations; and a root ang.json with features on. *.local.* files are left out because a clone never carries them
knowns.answers: What does the fixture repo's seed contain, and how is it generated? Zac's call: generated with a library such as faker, never written by an LLM, because reasoned content could carry sensitive training data into a public repo. Still open: which local edits, rules, settings and project-context/ docs make a representative instance, and whether a seeded generator script reproduces it deterministically

decisions.decision: Install by copy-in of src/ (giget/degit --force) wrapped in a shipped install.sh, so the install is one copy-pasteable line. The script protects the user's .claude/settings.json and carries future install changes to every new user (Zac's call)

No uninstall command: removing a vanilla install is deleting skills, rules and project-context/, and local workflow improvements make automating it unreliable. Easy by hand, hard to automate (Zac's call)

The upgrade skill is in scope for this epic and is to be built. Zac's deliberate exception to the intent's build-the-least: real value, and it belongs to the same logical unit of work as install, however big it has grown

install.sh merges an existing .claude/settings.json with node (already required, no jq dependency) and first keeps a backup of the user's original, in case the merge drops properties that mattered (Zac's call)
Tests ship with installs: a local workflow improvement may change shipped scripts, and having the tests on hand lets the user run them to check (Zac's call)

giget stays, run through npx and pinned to giget@3.3.1; the README and docs list node with npm/npx as the prerequisite. Zac's call: node is already required, giget carries features we'd otherwise hand-roll, and documenting npm/npx beats also leaning on curl and tar inside the script

The install's settings merge favours the user: their values win, Ang adds only missing keys, arrays are unioned, and only the first backup (.claude/settings.json.pre-ang) is kept, so re-runs are no-ops. Spiked: the user's outputStyle, model, deny rule and hook all survived, with no duplicates on re-run

No pre-open-source upgrade path: the skill isn't designed around instances like ohnvm, because only Zac has them and only until he upgrades them. A missing version record never hard-stops an upgrade, so an LLM-run upgrade of ohnvm may succeed by accident (Zac's call)

The upgrade merges file by file, three-way, against the version.json SHA, with git merge-file, and never commits: the user reviews the unstaged result and commits or drops it. Four routes by conflicted-file count: fast (only one-sided changes), agent-resolved (any clean merge or 1-5 conflicts; the agent resolves them itself, no user input), guided (6-11; the agent resolves what it's sure of and confirms with the user only merges that risk breaking Ang or a user customisation), guided with warning (12+ or no version record; before writing, warn with the count and a risk assessment, suggest owning a fork, user decides, then as guided). Thresholds are named constants, tuned after rc.2 (Zac's call)

No local changelog of workflow improvements in v1: diffing the instance against the version.json SHA already shows what changed locally, and the user supplies the why during a guided merge. Parked with a wake condition (Zac's call)

Cutting a release is in scope for this epic: the repeatable process (stamp the tag into install.sh, tag, publish the generated GitHub Release, plus whatever u1 settles) belongs here, since install.sh and the upgrade skill consume releases (Zac's call)

install.sh checks before copying anything and stops with a plain message saying what's wrong and how to fix it: node >=26 (k9) and npx, inside a git repo and at its root (from a subdirectory it names the root to cd to, since /project-context/ links only resolve there), a clean working tree, Ang not already installed (points to upgrade), no collisions with existing project-context/ or same-named skills, rules or agents, settings.json parses, and the ref resolves (says which of network, rate limit or bad ref failed). On success it prints version, location and next step. No OS, disk or permission checks (Zac's call)

The upgrade skill checks before writing anything and stops with a plain message when: already on the target release, the target is older (downgrade), the working tree is dirty, or prerequisites are missing. A missing or unknown version record goes to guided with warning, not a stop (d8). It finishes with a from/to, clean-vs-judgement summary and how to review (Zac's call)

install.sh and the upgrade skill install and upgrade only to published releases, never a bare SHA or branch. The default target is the latest release, and an override must name a release tag. The resolved SHA is still recorded beside the tag as the merge base. Zac raised this during the install spike, and the upgrade guidance needs it: it is written per release (Zac's call)

A release skill that lives only in the Ang repo (it doesn't ship in src/) runs each release with Zac: preflight, gather, version, drafting the release notes and upgrade guide with him, the upgrade rehearsal, then commit, tag and push on his go. The prose is drafted by an LLM and edited with Zac, which is what open-source-hygiene d13's 'no hand-kept changelog' meant: nothing written from a blank page (Zac's call)

install.sh ships as a GitHub Release asset, stamped with TAG and SHA by the release job. The README one-liner pipes releases/latest/download/install.sh, and the repo copy is never stamped. Installs can only land on a published release (Zac's call)

v1.0.0 is the delivery intent's finish line: everything from the first commit to the close of the work now in flight. Before it there are only v1.0.0-rc.N pre-releases, as many as it takes to prove install, upgrade and release. No 0.x releases. Semver from v1 (Zac's call)

Zac alone decides when to release: no nudges, schedules or automatic releases. Preflight checks (unmerged streams, listed by name, CI, Node LTS bump, leftover drafts, the README one-liner) are warnings to eyeball, never blocks. Releases are cut from the head of main (Zac's call)

/cut-release commits, tags and pushes on Zac's explicit go, asked for immediately before; an earlier go doesn't count. It opens the draft release with gh release view --web, and Zac presses Publish himself in the web UI, then tells the skill. gh is a release-only dependency on Zac's machine (Zac's call)

Drafting is fed by a deterministic release-manifest script (src/ changes with renames, commits, archived epics, 10k changes, settings diff since the last tag) read by a release-scout agent, with a coverage check that every manifest entry lands in the notes, the guide or an 'internal' list. No commit conventions, changeset files or PR labels (Zac's call)

Thinking work (gather, version, drafts) runs in the local /cut-release skill. Mechanical work runs in a GitHub Actions job on v* tag push: tests, install smoke test on a fresh repo, stamp install.sh, gh release create --draft (Zac agreed)

Upgrade rehearsals run against a dedicated seeded fixture repo, not ohnvm: an install with typical local edits, upgraded to each candidate before release. After each publish, the real upgrade is committed and tagged there, leaving room for multi-version-jump tests later (Zac's call)

Zac decides every version number. /cut-release proposes one with its reasons, and he accepts or revises it. Guidelines, not rules: major when a user must act or their way of working changes, minor for features and file moves the upgrade guide handles silently, patch for fixes (Zac's call)

Repo-only skills and agents sit beside the shipped ones without shipping: the root .claude/skills and .claude/agents become real folders that symlink each src/ entry one by one, plus the repo-only entries. Repo-only scripts (release-manifest, the link script) live in a root scripts/ folder instead, so .claude/scripts stays a whole-folder symlink (Zac's call)

Release notes are written in Zac's public voice from 10k voice-and-attribution: conversational, opinionated, humorous with a bit of whimsy, trimmed, not corporate, with an emoji per heading. Breaking changes and fixes stay plain-spoken. The upgrade guide has no voice: it's for an agent (Zac's call)

Upgrades are all or nothing: no partial upgrades, so every upgrade ends in a stable state and version.json always names one release. Guided with warning says how big the upgrade is and the user decides whether to go ahead. Partial upgrades are parked with a wake condition (Zac's call: a feature nobody has asked for, and its version record needs per-file bases)

Each release rehearses only the upgrade from the previous release. Users jumping several majors upgrade one major at a time, naming each release tag as the target; d14's tag override and d13's no-downgrade stop already allow that, with latest as the default target. Rehearsals that skip releases are parked until the first minor or patch release (Zac's call: while every release is a major, every upgrade is breaking anyway)

A default install makes no GitHub API call: the release asset's stamp carries TAG and SHA. A tag override calls GET /releases/tags/{tag}, which resolves the SHA and checks it's a published release. The repo's own install.sh is unstamped and stops without a tag argument, pointing at the release-asset one-liner (Zac's call)

An upgrade runs the target release's merge engine, fetched at the target tag, not the installed one's, so merge fixes reach users on the upgrade that ships them and the engine always reads the target's upgrade guide format (Zac's call)

Zac turns on immutable releases once, by hand. No v* tag ruleset: immutable releases already lock published tags, and a ruleset would only guard the unpublished window as insurance against a hypothetical, while blocking deletes would break the delete-and-recut path for a failed release run. A broken release or install.sh is fixed only by a patch release, never by editing a published asset (Zac's call)

The delivery intent ends at the first public release, v1.0.0, the point where Zac announces Ang on socials, not at the first tag. rc pre-releases weren't considered when the intent was written and don't end it. The next intent comes later, when Zac wants a new feature or issues and PRs prompt one (Zac's call)

The release process, fixture repo and upgrade skill are within the intent's and business constraints' 'bare minimum', which means the minimum for a process that is comfortable to maintain and operate, not the least effort or fewest dependencies. No exception or ADR is needed (Zac's call)
upgrade-ang is plumbing, like install.sh and the release pipeline, not a fifth feature, so what-ang-is stays at four features (Zac's call)

The upgrade finds the guides in (installed, target] by following each guide's from: line back from the target's guide, fetched raw at the target tag, so no GitHub API call lists releases. A wrong from: line breaks the chain, and the fixture rehearsal catches it before release (Zac agreed)

version.json is read and written only through core 'version show' and 'version write' commands in the library script, which install.sh and upgrade-ang both use, so there is one record format and one place to test it (Zac agreed)

upgrade-ang and the upgrade engine ship in v1.0.0-rc.1, so the fixture (an rc.1 install) already has the skill for the rc.1 to rc.2 rehearsal; only the engine comes from the target. rc.1 waits on the upgrade stories in exchange for a rehearsal that follows the real user path (Zac's call)

Ang supports macOS, Linux and Windows through WSL, where install.sh, Claude Code and Node 26 all run inside WSL, and install.sh stops under Git Bash, MSYS or Cygwin. Native Windows is untested and best effort: it needs Git for Windows (Claude Code runs Ang's hooks and Bash commands in Git Bash) and the documented manual install. Shell-free hooks are parked (Zac's call)
